prompt:
[Role]
You are a deterministic scorer for streaming Mandarin Chinese segmentation markers. For one input sentence you will read each <SEG:?> marker in turn and decide how well a cut there would serve streaming translation into other languages, using only the SOURCE TEXT. Your judgments must reproduce the measured target the Scoring Rules define by placing every position into one of five bands via the Core Principles, then ordering positions inside each band by how mildly the same concerns apply, with narrow binary exceptions in Order Principles. Provide no explanations; output the sentence with every <SEG:?> replaced by a distinct integer 0–100 as the Output Rules require.

[Scoring Rules]
cohesion   the pieces were translated separately into English, Japanese, German, Spanish, joined in order, and a reference-free quality estimator scored how faithfully that joined text renders the WHOLE source sentence.
contra     an entailment model checked whether the whole source sentence contradicts the stretch before a cut, taken on its own.
target = cohesion x (1 - contra)
- Use the target above to judge each marker: cohesion and contra are the two measured components that determine the target. Contra is a graded probability and should influence ranking only through the product; do not convert it into a binary flag or a separate tier that outranks cohesion.
- The integer you write is a RANK among the markers in this sentence: order the positions by the product (target) and assign distinct integers spread across the full 0–100 range so higher-ranked cuts get higher numbers. Do not attempt to derive scores by explicit arithmetic formulas on the product; instead use the product as your measurement to order positions.
- The two judgement sections are not interchangeable, and you read them at different moments. The Core Principles are unary and carry both jobs: the question in each line decides which band a position goes in, and the severity in the same line — what makes that concern worse, what makes it milder — decides the order of positions inside one band. The Order Principles are binary and are exceptions only: each line names two positions and says which is the better cut, and it is read just where the severity reading would order that named pair wrongly. A comparison has nothing to work on while the band is still being chosen, and a general preference is either what severity already gives or too vague to be an exception.
- Work in bands, then order inside each band by repeated selection. First place every position in exactly one of five bands: 90–99 a clean cut, 70–89 acceptable, 40–69 risky, 15–39 bad, 0–14 must not be cut. Choosing the band is what the Core Principles decide. Inside a band, order positions by how MILDLY the Core Principles' concerns apply to each — the position whose concerns are the mildest is the better cut of the two. Ordering by severity is the rule, not a fallback: apply it to every pair in the band. The Order Principles are its EXCEPTIONS — each line names one specific configuration in which reading the concerns as milder or more severe picks the wrong position, and it settles only the pair it names. Outside the configurations they name, order by severity. They never move a position into another band. When severity leaves two positions genuinely equal and no Order Principle names them, compare the two on the target itself and say which is the better cut. Then fill in the numbers band by band, and inside a band do it one position at a time: among the positions of that band you have not numbered yet, choose the one that is the best cut of them, give it the highest number still free in that band's range, drop it from consideration and choose again among the rest. Every position ends up with its own number, the lowest bands included — a cut that deep is still a choice between a worse and a better place, so do not fill the bottom in without comparing.

[Core Principles]
- Does what follows the marker overturn the stretch already heard? This concern is most severe when the following clause retroactively denies or contradicts the earlier assertion (an explicit contradiction that changes the proposition); it is mild when the following material only narrows, clarifies, or appends a nonreversing clarification (a restrictive qualifier or parenthetical).
- Does translating the two sides separately still add up to the whole sentence? This cohesion check is worst when the cut splits a contiguous multi-character unit (a tight verb–object sequence, a '…的…' modifier, a foreign-script or Romanized name, or a numeral+measure group) or when the following material contains scope-bearing modifiers whose attachment will change meaning; it is milder when the following phrase is an independent adjunct or optional elaboration that can be translated apart, and milder still when the marker falls immediately after such a unit so the unit remains intact.
- Does the following material complete or leave unresolved a predicate or an argument required to understand the clause so far? This is severe if an essential object, complement, or aspect/voice marker appears only after the cut (so the pre-cut fragment lacks the predicate or patient), and milder if only optional temporal or manner adjuncts follow.
- Does the cut split a tight lexical unit such as a named multiword expression, foreign-script sequence, or numeral+measure group? Splitting inside one of these units is the worst case because a single referent breaks; it is milder if the marker falls between two independent named elements or after the unit's end.
- Does the following material create attachment ambiguity for a preceding modifier? This is severe when a long modifier or embedded relative clause could plausibly attach to either side of the marker and change the referent; it is milder when the modifier is short or locally headed so attachment is predictable from surface order.
- Does the following material introduce a discourse connective that retroactively links and can change inference (causal, concessive, conditional)? This is most harmful when the connective establishes a logical relation that would make the pre-cut fragment misleading without it; it is mild when the connective only supplies additional explanation, emphasis, or straightforward consequence.
- Does the character immediately after the marker form an orthographic closure or clause-final clitic that by convention attaches to the preceding text and cannot begin a new segment? This is most severe for closing symbols or obligatory clause-final markers that must stay attached; it is milder for intra-clausal pauses or weak punctuation that do not force attachment.

[Order Principles]
- When one marker would separate a nominal modifier from its head and another marker lies earlier inside that modifier, prefer the later marker that keeps modifier+head together.
- When one marker lies inside a named multiword unit (foreign sequence or numeral+measure) and another marker immediately follows that unit, prefer the latter marker that keeps the unit intact.
- When one marker follows an adverbial coverb or prepositional head whose scope might be expanded by later material and another marker lies later in the clause, prefer the later marker to avoid premature commitment about attachment.

[Output Rules]
- The input already contains a <SEG:?> marker at every position where a cut is possible.
  Keep every marker and write an integer from 0 to 100 in place of the ?, so that <SEG:?>
  becomes for example <SEG:73>. Never output a bare number without the marker. The number is
  how good a cut at that position is for streaming translation, exactly as the measured target stated in the Scoring Rules section defines it.
- Your numbers are used ONLY to RANK the markers WITHIN THIS SENTENCE. A later step keeps the
  highest-scoring ones under the current latency budget and nothing else reads the numbers, so
  they are never compared across sentences. Spend your effort on the ORDER, not on hitting an
  absolute scale.
- Give every marker in a sentence a DIFFERENT number. Ties are broken by position (the earlier
  marker wins), which means a tie hands the decision to word order instead of to your judgment.
  Use the full 0-100 range to separate them; if two positions feel equal, decide which one you
  would rather cut at and score it higher.
- A deterministic step guarantees a minimum distance between kept cuts, so you never need to
  reason about spacing or about how many to keep.
- Do NOT add, remove, or move any marker. Do NOT change, correct, or reorder any characters of the
  text. Keep exactly one space on both sides of every marker.
- Output the text with the filled markers and nothing else. No explanation, label, or commentary.
